name: Alex m. mulinge
feedback: D1 is the strongest part of this submission. You catalogued nine of the ten planted findings with a class, a CWE, and a quoted evidence line for each: SQLi (A03/CWE-89 with the admin' OR '1'='1 capture), unsalted MD5 (CWE-328 is a defensible variant of the weak-hash class), alg:none (CWE-345 reads fine), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019, missing exp/nbf, the stored XSS beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443, XXE, path traversal to /etc/passwd, and open redirect. What you missed was the cookie finding, the missing Secure and SameSite flags around line 86, which is the tenth finding and the easy fourth member of the access-control set. The bigger problem is the decoy: the intended safe construct was the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals(), which is constant-time and therefore sound, with the b64url helpers as the supporting safe encoding. You instead nominated the JWT role claim, and while your reasoning there is coherent and you correctly kept alg:none as a real bug, that is not the planted decoy, so that row earns very little. D2 has solid per-hop PoCs and complete CVSS vector strings, which many submissions lack, but two things hold it back. The chain is never reconciled to the capture timeline, there are no timestamps such as 02:15:31 for the SQLi or 02:24:02 for the file read, and you left the stored XSS (02:18:47) and open redirect (02:21:13) hops out of the chain entirely. Your SQLi vector also reads CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H for 9.8, but the authentication bypass does not touch availability, so it should be A:N giving roughly 9.1. Only findings 1 to 3 carry a justifying sentence; 4 through 9 are bare scores. The business impact names 312 customers but stops there, with no naira figure and no stated assumptions about balances up to around 950k NGN summing to tens of millions, which is the row that separates a number from real impact. D3 is a clean, readable leadership report with a good threat model and findings tied to evidence, but it inherits the wrong decoy, and the remediation section is labelled Ranked by Risk Reduction per Hour of Effort while the actual order tracks CVSS severity rather than effort to risk, which caps that row at half. Your four detection rules give exact log fields and patterns, which is good, but none of them state a false-positive rate, so they fall short of the stopgap bar. The exec summary also does not land on a customers-and-naira headline. D4 is genuinely strong: you answer all four prompts in your own voice, cite Canon 1 and Canon 2 by number and use them, and you anchor the reasoning to your own evidence about separating proof from assumption. The one gap is the NDPA, you reference accountability in the abstract but never name the section, which needed to be section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying the 312 data subjects on high risk. I looked hard for a way to push this into the 70s and the evidence did not support it, because the decoy is wrong in both D1 and D3, the chain has no timestamp reconciliation, and the impact carries no naira. There is no fabrication here, every evidence line traces to the pack, so nothing was penalised. The single most important fix is to reconcile your exploit chain hop by hop to the actual capture timestamps and convert the 312-record exposure into a naira impact with stated assumptions, because that is what turns a competent finding list into a report leadership can act on.
